News.title: I’ve been forced to rip down children’s play park & marquee by killjoy council – 1000s back me… I’ll be forced to close
News.content:
PLAY PARK PROTEST I’ve been forced to rip down children’s play park & marquee by killjoy council – 1000s back me… I’ll be forced to close

A LANDLORD could be forced to tear down a children’s play area and a marquee by the local council.

He says thousands of people support him and he’ll be forced to close for good if he can’t keep them.





Campaigners launched a 3,000-strong petition to save the marquee, decking and children’s area at the pub.

Planners ordered the structures to be removed because the land at Castell y Bwch Inn hadn’t been granted consent for food and drink.

But landlord Gary Bulmer has submitted a planning application describing it as essential for the pub’s survival in Cwmbran, South Wales.



Torfaen Borough Council had served an enforcement notice on the previous tenants in 2022 outlining the established boundaries for food and drink use.

Mr Bulmer says describes those boundaries are “poorly researched and inconsistent.”

He argues the land has been in A3 use for more than 10 years and the application should be approved.

The planning statement warns the council would have to take Mr Bulmer to court to establish the boundaries.



It said: “Restricting this to the boundaries defined in the 2022 enforcement action would have such a detrimental impact upon the sustainability of the Inn that it would be forced to close.

“Consequently, this cannot be considered a viable option by the applicant.”

The council’s next option would be to prosecute the applicant, which they can only do if they believe that it is in the public interest to do so.

“Given that a recent petition has seen more than 3,000 signatures, most of which are local, supporting both the decking area and the location of the children’s play area, and that if successful the inn would still be forced to close leading to the loss of the community facility, it is doubtful that this would be considered a viable option by the council.”

The statement also acknowledges the site has “an extremely complex history and that there are no clear-cut solutions to the current situation”.



The application added: “It is considered that all this land needs to be utilized for A3 use for the inn to remain financially viable, and should this application be refused, the inn will almost certainly be forced to close, with the loss of another community facility and jobs within Torfaen.”

The application is being considered by the planning department.

The Sun Online has attempted to contact Torfaen Borough Council.

News.title: Farce as HMS Dragon forced into Med port after suffering maintenance issue as warship runs into more trouble
News.content:
THE HMS Dragon has been forced to make port in the Mediterranean due to a “maintenance issue” as the warship faces further problems.

The vessel’s staff worked around the clock to get the destroyer ready after it was scrambled into action from dry dock earlier last month.





The ship was covered in scaffolding, without any missiles and midway through a planned maintenance, when RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus was struck by a drone.

Sir Keir Starmer had faced fierce criticism over the sluggish deployment of HMS Dragon to protect the major British base as the conflict in Iran rages on.

But the destroyer – which only arrived weeks after the fighting kicked off – is now heading away from the front line.

The Ministry of Defence has revealed that the HMS has sailed to a safe berth to undergo repairs, according to the MailOnline.

The stop will reportedly include attending to what officials described as “a minor technical issue with onboard water systems”, the outlet reports.

The MoD said that the vessel would retain a “very high level of readiness” and would be “able to sail at short notice if required”.

It is currently unclear where exactly HMS Dragon is or what port it is going into for security reasons.



However, the UK has naval bases on Cyprus and Gibraltar in the region.

Defence insiders insisted there’s no crisis onboard, saying the crew have had full access to food and water throughout as the HMS temporarily withdraws.

They also stressed the stop-off had been planned in advance at “roughly this stage” of the deployment.

HMS Dragon took a week to get to sea, a further three days to leave British waters, four days to call in Gibraltar and six to span the Mediterranean.

Families gathered on the dockside as the Type 45 Destroyer left Portsmouth Harbour on March 10.



The warship finally arrived in Cyprus in the last week of March.

The air defence destroyer joined US and French warships to defend the eastern Mediterranean from Iranian missiles and drones.

The Sun reported at the time that five out of six of the Royal Navy’s £1billion destroyers were in port being repaired while the RAF base in Cyprus came under attack.

The MoD had told MPs that the HMS Dragon was “operational” which means it should have been ready to sail in no more than 72 hours.



But her sailing came a week after Sir Keir Starmer ordered her to sea – and ten days after the strike on the Cypriot base.

The sluggish response saw the ship engulfed in a row over Britain’s readiness to respond to a crisis – and the seemingly small size of the Royal Navy.

The latest setback comes amid growing embarrassment, with US President Donald Trump and his War Secretary Pete Hegseth taking repeated swipes at the Royal Navy.

Trump has slammed Sir Keir’s wavering response to the conflict more than once in the past month.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said of the latest development: “HMS Dragon is undertaking a routine logistics stop and a short maintenance period in the Eastern Mediterranean allowing the ship to take onboard provisions, optimise systems and conduct maintenance.



“HMS Dragon will remain at a very high level of readiness during the period, able to sail at short notice if required.

“The UK continues to maintain a robust and layered defensive presence in the Eastern Mediterranean working in coordination with allies.

“This includes Typhoon and F-35 jets, Wildcat and Merlin helicopters and advanced counter-drone and air defence systems.”

The Royal Navy’s Type 45 destroyers, like HMS Dragon, have Britain’s best air defence missiles.

Their radars can track 1,000 objects from 250 miles away and blast up to eight missiles simultaneously to intercept targets.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Two additional Merlin Crowsnest helicopters have also arrived in Cyprus.

UK Typhoons and F-35 jets, supported by Voyager refuelling and Royal Navy Merlin and Wildcat helicopters have also continued their defensive missions across the region.

News.title: US journalist who was abducted in Iraq after armed men stopped car on street and kidnapped her to be released
News.content:
A KIDNAPPED American journalist who worked for the BBC will be released, according to Iraqi armed group Kataib Hezbollah.

Shelly Kittleson was abducted on March 31 from a street corner in Baghdad by an Iranian-backed Iraqi armed group.





Shocking footage from local media showed Kittleson being grabbed by armed thugs and pulled into a car – sparking a frantic rescue operation.

Kataib Hezbollah had not claimed responsibility for the brutal snatching of the American journalist until now – though US and Iraqi officials had blamed the group.

The group said in a statement today that Kittleson must leave Iraq immediately when she is released.

It claimed the decision to free the journalist was made because of the patriotic stances taken by the outgoing Iraqi PM Mohammed Shia al-Sudani.

Kataib Hezbollah did not give further details, but added that it was a one-time gesture that would not be repeated.

Kittleson is a freelance journalist who previously worked for the BBC.

A US citizen currently based in Rome, the brave correspondent is known for her war reporting from Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria.



Harrowing footage showed her being bundled into a car by armed men near Baghdad Hotel on Saadoun Street.

After her capture at the end of March, cops launched a recovery mission.

They arrested one suspect and seized a vehicle used by the gunmen, and reportedly chased four of the armed men driving away while Kittleson was still in a car.

They later found an overturned vehicle that was thought to have flipped as the gangsters tried to flee – but the journalist was not inside.

Kittleson’s emergency contact Alex Plitsas, CNN national security analyst, confirmed her capture in a statement on X.



He wrote: “I can confirm that my friend Shelly Kittleson was abducted and may have taken hostage in Baghdad by Khatib Hezbollah.”

Kataib Hezbollah – the group that kidnapped Kittleson – is the most powerful of the Shiite, Iran-backed groups that hold sway in Iraq.



The abduction is thought to have been part of an alleged plot to capture or kill female journalists.

He later told CBS that Kittleson had been warned by the US government about a specific threat to her from Iran-backed paramilitaries.

Plitsas said his friend had been warned that her name was on a list in the militia’s possession.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A second source confirmed that the journalist had been told of a risk, but thought it was false information.

Plitsas described Kittleson “one of the kindest people” who “doesn’t have a mean bone in her body”.

News.title: World’s drinking capital where kids as young as 12 are hooked, pints are served as breakfast & 22 people die every DAY
News.content:
AN ELDERLY man sits alone at a terrace table as he waits for the waitress to bring him his “best friend”.

Sitting outside in -3C, 58-year-old Mihai smokes a cigarette at the cheap neighbourhood bar at noon as he waits for a glass of £2.50 vodka and a pint of beer for 50p as he starts his day in the world’s drinking capital.



“Booze is my best friend, booze is my breakfast,” he says at the pub in Pitesti, Romania – now labelled the “drunkest country on Earth”.

Mihai adds that he usually binges in a group from around midday onwards – and that many feel encouraged to knock back pint after pint thanks to the incredibly cheap prices.



At supermarkets, a pint of beer can set you back just 50p.

Meanwhile, shoppers have to fork out just £3 for a bottle of white wine – with the same amount getting punters a standard double spirit and mixer on nights out.

Mihai is just one of many Romanians who hit the bottle all day, every day.

But on average, Romanians are knocking back 17 litres of pure alcohol per year, with this sobering statistic from the World Health Organisation has crowned its 19 million citizens as the heaviest drinkers on the planet.

The figure works out at 750 beers a year – the equivalent of two pints every single day, with no breaks.



While the yearly figures might not sound staggering initially, what makes the alcohol consumption more dangerous in Romania is its high pecentage spirits, such as the country’s national drink, țuică, which can be as much as 55 per cent.

In fruit-picking areas, alcohol consumption levels are also higher, as many rural areas produce their own booze, meaning potency is more difficult to control.

This can pose severe health risks, especially long-term, such as liver damage, heart problems and even dementia.

The country has seen a rise in alcohol consumption over the last decade, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), with a sudden jump post-pandemic.

The consequences are deadly – a study by the European Commission estimates that around 8,000 Romanians die every year due to alcohol-related causes.



That means 22 Romanians every day – almost one every hour.

The toll is also feared to be higher by some experts who say there are further unrecorded alcohol-related deaths.

Romanians also displayed harmful bingeing patterns, having one of the highest levels of heavy episodic drinking rates in the world.

Many men are in and out of hospitals for years as they battle long-term health woes like liver damage to receiving treatment for severe injuries which have happened while intoxicated.

Scratch beneath the surface and you’ll find an even more disturbing reality.



Romanian men are drinking on a completely different level compared to women, consuming around 27 litres annually, or roughly 1,200 pints a year.

That’s more than three pints of beer a day, every day of the year.

By comparison, Brits get through about 10.8 litres per person, while in parts of the Middle East — where alcohol is restricted — consumption can fall to as little as 0.1 litres a year.



While Russia still leads the world in booze-linked deaths overall, Romania stands out for its relentless consumption levels.

On top of this, drinking in Romania isn’t just about what’s bought over the counter – it’s what’s brewed at home.

Across the country, powerful homemade spirits like țuică are widely produced, Madalina Cristea, who was born and raised in Bucharest, told us.

These spirits have folk songs dedicated to them, are often cheaply made and have little regulation covering them.

Some home-distilled batches can reach up to 65 per cent alcohol – and many Romanians get multiple shots down each day.



A parallel drinking culture exists in homes as opposed to in public settings – a private space where drinks are stronger, more accessible, and harder to track.

Madalina said: “There are some people I know, they drink whenever they go to a party, whenever they wake up in the morning… basically everyday living… It’s a cycle.”

In poorer rural areas, alcohol fills the gaps left by lack of jobs, services and opportunity.



High unemployment in the countryside and outside major cities drives many to drink to escape stress, boredom, and economic insecurity.

Studies show that in economically disadvantaged regions, heavy drinking is far more common.

Alcohol fuels unemployment while unemployment fuels alcohol abuse – a vicious cycle that hits the hardest in rural communities.

Kids drinking to ‘cope with stress’

Romanian kids are also being introduced to booze shockingly young – often by their own parents at home, where drinking is treated as totally normal rather than dangerous.

With alcohol easy to buy with barely enforced age limits widespread, it has become a rite of passage – turning kids as young as 12 into regular drinkers.



Save the Children Romania Program Manager Cristina Adam said alcohol consumption among young people had reached extremely worrying levels, even revealing that some kids use it to cope with stress.

She told us: “Alcohol is extremely socially normalised and easily accessible.

“At the same time, many teenagers experience stress, anxiety, and social pressure – with alcohol being used as a coping mechanism, not just as a form of entertainment.”

She added: “Children say that they have access to alcohol and can easily obtain it.”

Meanwhile, clinical psychologist Mihai Copaceanu said drinking from a young age was seen as a symbol of maturing – and a tool for youngsters to connect and achieve a “sense of well-being”.



“For teenagers, as a first sign of breaking away from childhood, alcohol consumption is the main reason they get together… it has a profound character of social cohesion and of achieving a state of well-being quickly,” he said.

“Many of my patients admit that they started drinking alcohol for the first time in their own families, with their parents’ consent, sometimes together with them.”

He added: “In Romania, it is very easy to buy alcohol and consume it in bars/restaurants even if you are under 18.

“So we have several explanations that differentiate us as a country, unfortunately.”

Copaceanu highlighted how the age of initiation in Romania had dropped significantly to as young as 12 – increasing the risk of problematic consumption and addiction.



He said: “I meet 15- and 16-year-olds in my office who admit that they are addicted to alcohol.”

Dr. Radu Tincu, a toxicologist at Floreasca Hostpial in Bucharest, said Romanian cultrue puts pressure on non-drinkers.

Refusing to booze is socially unacceptable, he said.

Sober-for-life locals are often labelled “sick” or “abnormal”, Dr Tincu said.



This mindset “puts pressure” on those who don’t want to consume alcohol to hit the bottle.

Booze is not treated as a vice – but rather a part of daily life.

Copaceanu echoed this sentiment – saying how alcohol is not perceived as a toxic substance, but rather as an integral part of culture.

The ex-WHO consultant said: “In Romania, when you visit someone, you are offered a glass of alcohol as a gesture of politeness… guests bring bottles of alcohol as gifts.

“Therefore, alcohol has a very strong social character in our country, and as long as we do not change this perception, we will not see a decrease in consumption.”



A Brit writer who has lived in Romania for 20 years, also told The Sun how alcohol was embedded deeply in the culture.

Deb Stowe said: “When I first moved here, I noticed that alcohol was on sale in places that you wouldn’t expect in the UK.

“Like in cinemas and in McDonald’s – just places that in the UK you wouldn’t associate with alcohol.”

Deb added: “If you go to someone’s house in the UK to visit them, they’ll probably say: ‘Would you like a tea?’

“Whereas here, if you go to visit someone in their home, they’ll almost certainly offer you alcohol.”



Romanian local Madalina added: “There’s a culture of drinking in Romania, especially in the countryside, where people usually, especially men, have, a shot of Țuică, which is the national drink.”

“They have a shot of that before lunch, supper, breakfast, you name it.”

Copaceanu also told how the country’s lack of alcohol policy and regulation also fed into the spiralling crisis.



“There are no national public health programs that would lead to a decrease in alcohol consumption,” he said.

Another major issue is with Romania’s healthcare system who only deal with very serious cases of alcoholism.

Doctors are taught to handle illnesses rather than provide support or treatment for addictions, experts say.

Trainee doctor Ioan Mirea says that even when people turn up begging for help they can often be turned away at the hospital gates.

He said: “Over half of our patients reach our gates and are escorted by the police as many are agitated and violent.”



For those who do receive treatment in the most severe cases, patients often need up to three weeks to get sober and cope with the withdrawal symptoms.

This can often hold up spare beds and leave other patients without help for longer.

Romania isn’t just drinking more than most of the world – it’s trapped in a cycle where cheap, strong alcohol, cultural acceptance and economic hardship fuel a crisis that kills thousands every year.

From homemade spirits to daily binge drinking, the problem runs deeper than statistics.

Until its roots are tackled, the World’s Booziest Country shows little sign of sobering up.

News.title: Moment thug points GUN at stunned chicken shop worker after he got wrong SAUCE in shocking attack
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a thug pointed a gun at a stunned chicken shop worker after he was given the wrong sauce.

Marwan Khadir, 18, flew into a rage after he was handed burger sauce instead of garlic mayo at the fast food shop in Penge, South London.





The teen was captured trying to clamber over the counter to attack the worker before whipping out the imitation firearm.

Khadir then pointed the realistic weapon at the victim, who was captured waving his hands around in fear.

He also threatened to shoot and kill the worker while still complaining about his order.

The thug then smacked the worker during the shocking attack on Christmas Eve last year.

Khadir has now been jailed for three years after he pleaded guilty to possessing an imitation firearm with intent to cause fear of violence, making threats to kill and assault occasioning Actual Bodily Harm (ABH).

Woolwich Crown Court heard the teen had rowed with his local chicken shop worker as he demanded three garlic sauces and three mayonnaises.

The footage showed Khadir sat in his living room counting out the sauces before phoning the shop up and complaining.



He then burst back into the restaurant, shouting: “I asked for three garlic and three mayos… You gave me four burger sauces.”

The attack saw the worker assaulted repeatedly as Khadir tried to get back behind the counter.

Police tracked the yob down through CCTV and seized the replica gun Khadir used in the attack, as well as fake ammunition.

Detective Sergeant Amy Cross, who led the investigation, said: “The tireless work by officers on this case over the Christmas and New Year period is further evidence that policing never stops, and their efforts ultimately led to a conviction.

“All our thoughts continue to remain with the victim of this terrifying ordeal, something no one should ever have to go through, let alone at their place of work. The strength he has shown since the attack has been remarkable.



“On top of this, the courage he demonstrated in coming forward and reporting the assault was incredibly brave. He was then able to subsequently identify the perpetrator, a crucial moment in allowing us to move the investigation forward.”

News.title: Mum’s mid-air birth on flight sparks debate over what baby’s citizenship will be – as expert reveals worst-case scenario
News.content:
AIR-BORN Mum’s mid-air birth on flight sparks debate over what baby’s citizenship will be – as expert reveals worst-case scenario

A BABY’s citizenship is left in limbo after the child was born mid-air on a flight between Jamaica and the United States.

The passenger went into labour on the Caribbean Airlines flight on April 4 and delivered her baby minutes before landing at John F. Kennedy Airport.



The plane was travelling from Kingston to New York when it gained an unexpected extra passenger.



The unusual birth circumstances have opened up a big debate over the child’s nationality.

The immigration lawyer and YouTuber Brad Bernstein said: “A baby born on a plane to NYC raises one big legal question… is that child automatically a US citizen?

“The answer depends on where the plane was at the exact moment of birth”, he added.

In a shock revelation, Bernstein said: “In some rare cases, a child born mid-flight could even end up stateless”.

Another YouTube lawyer suggested that citizenship might depend upon the nationality of the mother, as well as the airspace the baby was born in.

Usually, the baby takes on the nationality of the mother, but the US’s “right of soil” laws mean that anyone born on US ground – or airspace – can claim American citizenship.

So far, the nationality and citizenship of the newborn are not yet known.

Staff onboard the plane radioed in to air traffic control to request an early landing slot, saying: “We’ve got a pregnant passenger who is going into labor at this time”.



“Is it out yet?” air traffic control asked, to which the onboard staff member confirmed it was.

“Tell her she’s got to name it Kennedy,” the controller joked.

Mother and child received medical attention on the ground, but the condition of the pair has not been made public.

In a statement to Sky News, Caribbean Airlines commended the professionalism of their crew for managing the unexpected situation in accordance with established procedures, keeping both mother and child safe.

Caribbean Airlines have been contacted for further comment.



Births aboard planes are relatively rare as people who are over 32 weeks into their pregnancy must obtain medical clearance before travel.

One woman however gave birth to her bundle of joy on a flight from London to India, two months earlier than expected.

The passenger began experiencing stomach cramps shortly after take off.

Luckily, there were two doctors and four nurses aboard who stepped in to help the birth.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Air India paid for the return flight and thanked their crew and medical professionals for their excellent service aboard the plane.

News.title: Russia threatens to blow up iconic UK bridge in revenge for British drones destroying Putin’s key crossing
News.content:
RUSSIA has threatened to blow up Westminster Bridge in revenge for British drones destroying Putin’s key crossing in occupied Ukraine.

Spectacular footage captured the moment explosions rocked the critical structure which crosses over a distributary of the Dnipro called the Konka.





The strike was in March last year but it is now revealed Ukraine deployed British Malloy T-150 heavy-lift drones to wreak havoc on the bridge.

And the revelation has infuriated the Russians.

Moscow state media propagandist and British “expert” Vladimir Kornilov slammed the British for “openly” boasting about “their participation in acts of sabotage on Russian territory.”

The explosion was on Ukrainian territory under international law – though invaded by Putin.

Kornilov fumed: “It’s high time we started bragging: ‘Russian missiles destroyed the key Westminster Bridge’.

“Of course, the Houthis or the Iranians will be the ones doing the hitting!”

Branding the breakthrough mission a “terrorist attack”, Kornilov asked what the British would “sing about” if Westminster Bridge was destroyed.



The crossing, next to the Houses of Parliament, has long been a focus of Russian interest.

A picture shows Putin glamour spy Anna Chapman on Westminster Bridge before she was detained in New York by the FBI, and soon stripped of her UK citizenship.

Another Putin-loyal outlet, Tsargrad, declared: “The British are literally gushing with delight about their direct involvement in the terrorist attack.

“Isn’t it time to shift the strikes to the decision-making centre after such a candid admission?”

The explosion on the Konka bridge was – at the time – believed to be a straightforward aerial hit.



But now the secret is out that Ukraine’s innovative 426th Unmanned Systems Regiment used the heavy-lifting drone on more than 30 missions over 60 days.

The weapon delivered a staggering 1.5 tons of explosives while eluding Russian forces.

“Bridges are relatively easy to destroy from underneath,” said Ukrainian Col. Oleksii Bulakhov, the regiment’s commander.

“But they are engineered in a way that makes them extremely robust from the outside.”

The operation was carried out to curb Vladimir Putin‘s ability to strike Kherson in Ukraine.



Kyiv had tried to destroy it multiple times in the past with strikes and even US-made HIMARS rockets – but their attempts failed.

Ukrainian commanders eventually handed the operation to the innovative 426th Unmanned Systems Regiment – a unit known for cutting-edge drone warfare.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A 50kg shaped charge was lowered by cable onto the bridge’s weakest points.

A missile then ignited the explosives in one of the great operations of the four-year war.

News.title: Major UK airport is evacuated with flights delayed & passengers stuck on planes after ‘smoke inside terminal’
News.content:
TERMINAL TURMOIL Major UK airport is evacuated with flights delayed & passengers stuck on planes after ‘smoke inside terminal’

A MAJOR UK airport has been evacuated with emergency services attending the scene.

Passengers at Birmingham Airport have been forced to leave the North Terminal following reports of a fire in the baggage and immigration area.





West Midlands Fire Control said multiple fire crews were on the scene following reports of smoke.

On social media, images show crowds of people standing outside the building while emergency crews attend the scene.

One witness said the area had been “very smoky”.

Vicky said: “Arrivals and baggage area was very smoky, chemical-like.



“Bags were still being off loaded. Then alarms went off and we were evacuated.”

Meanwhile, passengers have shared pictures stuck in their plane seats as aircraft are being held airside.

Passengers have been told to stay put as emergency personnel investigate the fire incident.

To ensure everyone’s safety, evacuation was taken as a precautionary measure.



A Birmingham Airport spokesperson said: “We are aware of an incident affecting baggage reclaim and immigration in the North Terminal.

“We are working with emergency partners and as a precaution, passengers have been evacuated from this area only.

“The safety of our people and passengers is our number one priority and further updates will be provided.”

While there are limited details about the incident, it is thought the rest of the airport is operating as normal.

One Ryanair passenger said he had been stuck on his plane since landing at 1pm.



Martin Pawar, stranded on the runway, said: “Our Ryanair plane landed at 1pm from Girona in Spain. I’m sitting on the runway. Nobody is allowed to leave the plane.

“A stewardess has told us there is still no news and we are to remain on the plane.”

News.title: Chef fired for serving food that had fallen on floor wins £28,400 compensation
News.content:
Chef fired for serving food that had fallen on floor wins £28,400 compensation

A Thai restaurant chef who worked for over 10 years was unfairly dismissed after allegations of serving floor-dropped food, with the Workplace Relations Commission awarding him €32,550 (£28,429)

View 2 Images The Workplace Relations Commission building in Lansdowne House, Dublin.

A Thai restaurant has been ordered to pay €32,550 (£28,429) in compensation to a chef who was dismissed after serving food that had fallen on the floor to a customer.

‌



The Workplace Relations Commission ruled that Ecoco Asian Kitchen, which runs outlets in Cornelscourt, Dublin and Bray, Co Wicklow, had wrongfully sacked chef Tommy Chee King Eng.

‌



The WRC heard that the chef had been employed by the company for more than 10 years before being let go on 25 June 2025, following allegations of food safety and hygiene violations.

‌



Mr Eng claimed he was dismissed for picking up food from the floor, which he subsequently cooked and served to a customer, as well as for using an incorrect technique when preparing roast duck.

View 2 Images The Workplace Relations Commission building in Lansdowne House, Dublin.

He told the WRC that he walked out of a disciplinary hearing when he was confronted with fresh allegations based on CCTV footage, reports the Irish Mirror.

‌



These related to claims that he was touching his head while cooking, failing to wear headwear, and using a mobile phone while preparing food.

The chef maintained he felt singled out, as other members of staff had engaged in similar behaviour without facing any disciplinary proceedings.

Mr Eng stated that no private space had been made available during the disciplinary process, with meetings taking place in a customer seating area and a cramped storeroom.

‌



A spokesperson for Ecoco Asian Kitchen said serious hygiene and food safety concerns had emerged in June 2025, shortly after the company had taken over running the restaurant. The firm stated it had suspended the chef on grounds of potential gross misconduct and subsequently dismissed him based on his written submissions.

It maintained it had adhered to fair procedures proportionate to a small employer.

However, WRC adjudication officer Breiffni O'Neill said the company's "reactive, backward-looking approach" was at odds with what would ordinarily be expected of a new owner inheriting a long-serving employee accustomed to existing practices.

‌



"In my view, a reasonable employer would have clearly communicated any revised standards, issued updated hygiene protocols, and offered refresher training with a reasonable period for adjustment," said Mr O'Neill.

He noted that the chef's explanations, including that the dropped food had been re-fried before being served, were not examined in a structured manner and the company had failed to provide any written communication of revised expectations.

"A reasonable employer, faced with such explanations, would have sought corroboration or clarification before concluding that they were inadequate," said Mr O'Neill.

‌



He argued the allegations "at their height" fell considerably short of the kind of serious and deliberate misconduct capable of justifying dismissal, "let alone summary dismissal."

The WRC stated the matters in question involved isolated lapses in food handling practice, none of which resulted in any customer complaint, harm or regulatory concern. While Mr O'Neill conceded that food safety and hygiene were serious concerns, he argued that warnings, retraining and closer supervision were ordinarily employed unless there was gross negligence, deliberate wrongdoing or actual harm.

He added: "Any reasonable employer would have considered proportionate corrective steps rather than proceeding directly to termination."

‌



Mr O'Neill stated that the procedures carried out by the company had progressed "at remarkable speed."

He further took issue with the absence of a suitable or private meeting space for the disciplinary hearing.

Conducting the meeting in a customer area and subsequently a cramped storeroom fell considerably short of the standard demanded by statutory fair procedure and natural justice, Mr O'Neill concluded.

‌



He also pointed out that the direct instruction to Mr Eng not to discuss the matter with any colleague without prior written authorisation directly contradicted being told he was free to bring a colleague to the disciplinary hearing.

"This contradiction is, frankly, bizarre, and it calls into question the respondent's bona fides in presenting itself as willing to facilitate colleague representation," said Mr O'Neill.

He highlighted that the company declined to amend a work roster to permit a colleague who had indicated he would accompany the chef to attend the meeting.

‌



The WRC additionally criticised the introduction of fresh allegations throughout the process and the failure to question the chef regarding them. Mr O'Neill noted that the involvement of the same two individuals representing the company throughout the entire process was also "a cause for grave concern."

He concluded it was equally unreasonable for the company to reject an appeal lodged by the chef's daughter on his behalf, given that English was not his first language.

Mr O'Neill stated that the absence of any functioning appeal process was "a significant procedural failing."

Article continues below

He ruled that the decision to sack the complainant was unjust, as it fell outside the range of responses expected of a reasonable employer.

The WRC ordered the company to pay the chef €30,150 in compensation for the unfair dismissal, along with a further €2,400 for failing to provide him with a minimum statutory notice period.

News.title: 'My son was killed protecting a friend - youth clubs are part of cure to knife crime epidemic'
News.content:
'My son was killed protecting a friend - youth clubs are part of cure to knife crime epidemic'

Writing for The Mirror as the Government's long-awaited knife crime strategy is published, Pastor Lorraine Jones Burrell says youth clubs are part of the cure to tackle unmet needs and lack of guidance young people face

View 2 Images Pastor Lorraine with her son Dwayne, who was stabbed to death in 2014 (Image: Pastor Lorraine Jones)

Youth clubs are not a luxury, they are a lifeline.

‌



In communities like ours, where young people are navigating trauma, poverty, exclusion, and the daily threat of violence, youth clubs represent safety, structure, and hope. Without them, we leave too many of our children exposed to exploitation, despair, and danger.

‌



That is why it matters that youth clubs are finally being recognised nationally as essential infrastructure, not optional extras. Through the Better Youth Spaces programme, the Government has committed to equipping, refurbishing and building hundreds of youth facilities across England, so more communities have the safe spaces young people desperately need.

‌



I speak not from theory, but from lived experience. My heart was shattered the day my son Dwayne was taken from me through knife crime. That pain never leaves you but I made a decision to turn that pain into power.

Major knife crime plan unveiled as grieving mum hails lifesaving measures READ MORE :

What I have witnessed again and again is that when young people are given safe spaces, trusted adults, and real opportunities, their lives can transform. Youth clubs provide more than activities - they provide belonging. They offer a place where young people are seen, heard, and valued. They are a place to heal from trauma, build confidence, and develop skills for a brighter future. Whether through mentoring, sport, education, or simply having a trusted person to talk to, these spaces save lives.

‌



I think of Tracy, who came through our doors at just 17 years old. She was a victim of county lines exploitation, frightened and hurting. When she arrived at Dwaynamics Boxing Gym, she was carrying trauma no child should carry. She told us a close friend had just been stabbed and killed and she feared she would be next. She said clearly, “I would be lost if I didn’t have Dwaynamics.” We wrapped our love, support, and belief around her.

Today, she has won several boxing awards and is now a carded amateur boxer with England Boxing. That is the power of a youth hub intervention, restoration, and transformation.

Programmes like Better Youth Spaces are about making sure stories like Tracy’s are not the exception. By investing in areas with the greatest need, they create safe third spaces where young people can access high quality activities, trusted adults and positive role models - all of which are key factors in diverting young people away from harm and criminality.

‌



Knife crime does not start with a weapon. It starts with unmet needs, pain, lack of guidance, lack of opportunity, and sometimes a lack of love.

Youth clubs directly address these root causes and interrupt the pathway to violence, including knife crime, by offering a positive alternative.

I welcome the commitment made by Sir Keir Starmer to tackle knife crime and invest in safer futures for our young people through the measures detailed in the government’s ‘Protecting Lives, Building Hope: A Plan to Halve Knife Crime’, which will be launched on Tuesday. From what I have seen, he is honouring his word and working across government to tackle harm and intervene early. This commitment must continue to reach the grassroots where it matters most.

Every young life is precious. Peace is possible but only if we give our young people somewhere safe to stand.

News.title: Major knife crime plan unveiled as grieving mum hails lifesaving measures
News.content:
Major knife crime plan unveiled as grieving mum hails lifesaving measures

The Home Office has unveiled its long-awaited knife crime strategy with measures to ramp up support for young people and new technology to help police pinpoint places and times to patrol

View 3 Images Pastor Lorraine Jones Burrell has welcomed the Government's focus on intervention (Image: David Dyson)

A grieving mum whose son was stabbed to death while trying to save a friend has welcomed new plans to tackle Britain's knife crime epidemic.

‌



Pastor Lorraine Jones Burrell told The Mirror that lives will be saved thanks to Labour's commitment to build and equip hundreds of youth facilities across England. On Tuesday the Home Office unveiled its long-awaited strategy to halve knife crime within a decade.

‌



New measures include ramping up the use of state-of-the-art mapping technology to identify hotspots, and scaling up the use of live facial recognition, knife arches and neighbourhood patrols.

‌



Meanwhile figures released on Tuesday show more than 3,000 additional police officers and Police Community Support Officers have been put into neighbourhood roles in less than a year.

Kanye West is BLOCKED from entering UK with Wireless Festival now cancelled READ MORE :

View 3 Images Pastor Lorraine with Idris Elba and Keir Starmer in 2024 (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

Pastor Lorraine's 20-year-old son Dwayne Simpson was killed in 2014, when he stepped in after seeing a friend being chased by a man with a knife. The church minister said: "My heart was shattered the day my son Dwayne was taken from me through knife crime. That pain never leaves you but I made a decision to turn that pain into power."

‌



Since the general election in 2024, knife crime has dropped by 8% and over 63,000 blades have been removed from circulation. The new strategy will see £26million ploughed into a Knife Crime Concentrations Fund - supporting 27 police forces whose areas account for 90% of knife crime in England and Wales.

It also includes plans to give 250 schools in hotspots specialist training and support to keep kids safe. There will also be 50 Young Futures Hubs in worst-affected areas by the end of the current Parliament. These will provide vital support and safe spaces for under-18s.

Pastor Lorraine, from Brixton, South London, said: "Knife crime does not start with a weapon. It starts with unmet needs, pain, lack of guidance, lack of opportunity, and sometimes a lack of love. Youth clubs directly address these root causes and interrupt the pathway to violence, including knife crime, by offering a positive alternative."

‌



View 3 Images Policing Minister Sarah Jones said state-of-the-art mapping would be a huge boost to forces (Image: Craig Connor/ChronicleLive)

Since her son's death aged just 20, she has helped support hundreds of youngsters at Dwaynamics Boxing Gym, set up by Dwayne and run in his memory. Pastor Lorraine said such projects show the power of early intervention - a key tenet of the Government's plan.

She said: "I think of Tracy, who came through our doors at just 17 years old. She was a victim of county lines exploitation, frightened and hurting.

‌



"When she arrived at Dwaynamics Boxing Gym, she was carrying trauma no child should carry. She told us a close friend had just been stabbed and killed and she feared she would be next. She said clearly, 'I would be lost if I didn’t have Dwaynamics.' We wrapped our love, support, and belief around her."

New mapping technology allows police to narrow down hotspots to just 100 square metres. This means they can pinpoint specific streets and times where the dangers are highest. This has been shared with police forces across England and Wales.

Crime and Policing Minister Sarah Jones said: “Knife crime devastates lives and families across the country – and the majority of it takes place on just a small number of streets across the country.

‌



“We will deploy state of the art mapping to identify these hotspots and target them with police patrols, Live Facial Recognition and knife arches to catch these criminals.

“This Government will halve knife crime within a decade, saving lives and protecting communities.”

The strategy focuses on supporting young people and stopping those at risk to turning to violence. More than £34million is committed to the County Lines Programme this year, aimed at disrupting drug networks and preventing exploitation.

Article continues below

There will also be £15million for the Ministry of Justice to carry out tailored interventions to steer young people away from further crime and violence. And £5.5million is being spent on embracing new technology to stop knife crime.

Nathaniel Peat, founder of The SafetyBox said: "Early intervention in schools is not optional, it is essential. If we are serious about changing outcomes for young people, we must invest in mental wealth, emotional resilience, and personal development before harm takes hold.

There is an urgent need to divert young people away from exploitation, violence, and knife crime, and toward structured, positive pathways. With the government’s plan, lasting change must start at the foundation."

News.title: Labour policing chief hits back over shoplifting - 'we're turning the tide'
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Labour policing chief hits back over shoplifting - 'we're turning the tide'

Policing Minister Sarah Jones said the Government is turning the tide against Britain's shoplifting epidemic, with a 21% rise in shop theft charges in a year

View 2 Images The Government says it is turning the tide over shoplifting

Labour's policing minister has said the Government is "turning the tide" on shoplifting after the number of thieves facing court action shot up.

‌



The Home Office said the number of criminal charges for shop thefts has risen by 21% in the past year. Policing Minister Sarah Jones told The Mirror the breakthrough means prolific offenders are finally facing the consequences of their actions.

‌



It comes after shocking scenes in Clapham saw shops ransacked by gangs of youths as part of a "link up" online trend the Government has pledged to tackle.

‌



Data shared with The Mirror shows there were 111,559 shop theft charges in the past year. Ms Jones said: "Shop theft isn’t low-level crime – it’s lawlessness that damages livelihoods and blights high streets. We’re turning the tide: more offenders are being charged, and we’re tightening the law so these criminals face real consequences.

Kanye West is BLOCKED from entering UK with Wireless Festival now cancelled READ MORE :

View 2 Images Policing Minister Sarah Jones said new laws will make it easier for officers to act (Image: Craig Connor/ChronicleLive)

“A small number of prolific offenders are driving a huge share of retail crime. We’re bringing policing, retailers and government together to target the worst perpetrators, cut reoffending, and make sure shopworkers and their customers feel safe.”

‌



Retailers said shoplifting cases had reached record levels thanks to a Tory loophole which meant thefts of less than £200 were unlikely to result in prosecution. Legislation making its way through Parliament will reverse this.

The Crime and Policing Bill will treat all shop theft offences as general theft – regardless of value – so harsher sentences will be at both the Magistrates and Crown Court’s disposal. The new laws will also make it a specific offence to assault retail workers.

Retailers have long warned that thieves, including organised gangs, are getting more brazen and staff face a rising threat of violence.

‌



Last week M&S retail director Thinus Keeve wrote in The Telegraph: "In the past week alone we have had gangs forcing open locked cabinets and stripping shelves, two men brazenly emptying the shelves of steak and walking out, a large group of young people ransacking a store before assaulting a security guard, a colleague headbutted trying to defuse a situation and another hospitalised after having ammonia thrown in their face."

He added: "We need to recognise this for what it is. A systemic issue. A growing issue. And one that demands a co-ordinated response across government, policing and industry."

The Met Police last week said six teenage girls had been arrested on suspicion of theft and assault in connection with two incidents in Clapham, south west London. These saw huge crowds of young people gather around shops and restaurants.

‌



Five people, including four police officers, were assaulted in scenes described by London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan as "appalling".

The Home Office said it will be focusing on most prolific offenders, with 9% of thieves accounting for 52% of all convictions.

Association of Convenience Stores chief executive Ed Woodall said: “The evidence shows that most shop theft is driven by a small number of prolific offenders who repeatedly target shops, often stealing goods to order.

Article continues below

“We welcome the government's continuing work with police and retail partners to prioritise bringing these prolific offenders to justice and stopping the damage they cause to high streets and local communities.”

News.title: 'Donald Trump's latest horrifying threat tells the enemy: 'It's your call''
News.content:
'Donald Trump's latest horrifying threat tells the enemy: 'It's your call''

Donald Trump threatened a "whole civilisation will die tonight" as he increasingly appears determined to unleash the full force of the American military if Iran does not open the Strait of Hormuz

View 3 Images Donald Trump has set a deadline for the Iranians to capitulate (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

A subtle sign nestled in Donald Trump's latest horrifying threat against Iran could be proof he has already lost the war in the Middle East, a body language expert has told the Mirror.

‌



Tetchy Trump once again threatened what remains of Iran's leadership to open the Strait of Hormuz ahead of his 8pm Eastern (1am Wednesday, UK time) deadline.

‌



Taking to his social media platform TruthSocial, the US President said a "whole civilisation will die tonight, never be brought back again."

‌



The post added: "I don’t want that ‌to ⁠happen, but it probably will. We ⁠will find out tonight, one of the most important moments ⁠in the long and complex history of ⁠the World."

View 3 Images Trump's post on TruthSocial has been widely condemned

Trump's latest tantrum was met with condemnation, including from presenter Piers Morgan who branded the statement as "a brazen pre-admission of genocide against the Iranian people, which would obviously be a war crime." The post will also add to increased criticism of Trump's handling of the war, which has seen the price of oil spike across the globe.

‌



While Trump's comments have sent a chill down the spines of many observers, body language expert Judi James told The Mirror the post appeared to be "hyperbolic" and could hint he has lost control of the war.

"Trump claims here that tonight will be 'one of the most important moments in the long and complex history of the World' and the enduring, historic legacy that will be left from this moment in time will be that sweary, grammatically-challenged post from the night before; the sight of him discussing the situation alongside the Easter bunny at a children's egg-roll and now this final warning of doom, where he uses social media to announce that 'A whole civilization will die tonight'," she said.

View 3 Images Trump has issued multiple threats against Iran (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



"Are there clues planted in the wording of this being a hyperbolic, brinkmanship threat aimed at achieving a sudden truce? Because Trump has also clearly opted to create a sense of indecision that seems to imply 'it's your call'.

"The word 'probably' in 'but it probably will' (happen); the words 'We will find out tonight' and the use of capitals for his 'WHO KNOWS?' seem crafted to suggest it is up to the other side here. You can almost see the shrug when he writes 'I don't want that to happen'.

"The tone of anger and frustration that saturated the previous post seems to have subsided here, but that doesn't mean this message reads any less chilling. It's hard to equate a social media post like this with the kind of terms and implications it implies. It's a method of communication we all normally use for less formal thoughts like wishing each other a Happy Easter or discussing reality TV shows, along with our GIFs and emojis, not to announce 'A whole civilization will die tonight'."

Article continues below

Trump's war against Iran has raged for more than a month and has been a clear demonstration of US military might. But Iran's remaining leadership has remained able to close the Strait of Hormuz, a major oil shipping lane.

News.title: Brits face 'snow eater' weather phenomenon as Met Office predicts 26C surge tomorrow
News.content:
Brits face 'snow eater' weather phenomenon as Met Office predicts 26C surge tomorrow

The Met Office says Tuesday is set to be the warmest day of the week - and possibly the hottest day of the year so far - with mercury soaring to 26C before turning 'markedly cooler'

View 2 Images The UK saw its hottest day of 2026 due to the Foehn effect (Image: Met Office)

Temperatures soared to almost 25C today - the hottest April on record - thanks to a little-known weather phenomenon that sucks up moisture and makes the air extremely dry and hot.

A toasty 24.8C was recorded in Mona, a small hamlet in Anglesey, Wales, this afternoon, while temperatures rose to 24C in the nearby coastal town of Porthmadog. "The very warm conditions in northwest Wales today have been in part, a result of a phenomenon known as the Foehn effect," the Met Office said.

The forecaster says temperatures are set to climb even higher to 26C tomorrow - possibly setting a new record for the hottest day of 2026 so far - before turning "markedly cooler" later in the week.

The Foehn effect is a weather phenomenon triggered by moist air forcing its way up the side of a mountain before cooling down and turning into clouds, causing rain or snow. By the time the air reaches the top, it loses most of its moisture.

View 2 Images A person sunbathing in Hyde Park today (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Then, as the air moves down the other side, it compresses and heats up rapidly, arriving in the valley below as a hot, dry wind - and causing temperatures in the area to soar.

"In the UK, the most notable Foehn events tend to occur across the Scottish Highlands where the moist prevailing westerly winds encounter high ground along Scotland's west coast," the Met Office says.

"This results in a marked contrast in weather conditions across the country with the west being subjected to wet weather, whilst the lower lying east enjoys the warmth and sunshine of the Foehn effect."

Fine and sunny weather will dominate parts of the UK over the coming days as warm air is drawn northwards, according to the Met Office.

Lighter winds on Wednesday will make things feel even warmer, particularly across central and southeast England, where temperatures could peak at 26C, it added. "These values are well above the early April average, which is typically in the mid-teens".

Northern Ireland and northwest Scotland will meanwhile see cool and cloudier weather, with outbreaks of rain at times.

Met Office Chief Forecaster Paul Gundersen said: "We're seeing a brief but notable spell of very warm weather for early April, with temperatures more typically associated with late spring or early summer. This could be the warmest spell at this point in April since 2020.

Article continues below

"However, this warmth will be short-lived, with a marked drop in temperatures and more unsettled conditions developing later this week. In some areas, daytime temperatures could fall by around 10°C between Wednesday and Thursday."

The US freelance reporter, based in the Middle East and Afghanistan, has featured in Foreign Policy, the BBC World Service, New Lines Magazine, Politico and Al Majalla, among other outlets, according to her X profile.

Shortly after she was taken on March 31, the Iraqi interior ministry said a female "foreign journalist was kidnapped by unknown individuals" in the capital Baghdad, adding that security forces are hunting down the perpetrators.

Kittleson was identified by Al-Monitor, one of the news outlets for which she has worked. She is believed to have been taken near the Palestine Hotel on Saadoun Street in central Baghdad, with her kidnappers heading southwest towards Babil province.

Footage shared by Al Arabiya appeared to show a woman being forced into a car by two men before the vehicle speeds off.

Middle East faces 'missile storm' if Trump steps up Iran attack

Iranian missile teams could unleash a terror storm of weapons against America, Israel and its Gulf allies if Trump carries out his 'wipe out civilisation' threat against the Tehran regime

View 8 Images The Middle East could face a huge Iranian backlash (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

US President Donald Trump threatened Iran’s ‘civilisation will die tonight’ as the Middle East braced for an Iranian backlash with a storm of missile strikes on neighbours.

‌



Gulf States Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar are bracing for a Trump-led escalation and Israel was also expecting a step-up in Iranian revenge attacks.

‌



Trump has threatened to bomb power plants, bridges, oil wells and water desalination plants, all illegal under international humanitarian law.

‌



And he warned: “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again. I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will. However, now that we have Complete and Total Regime Change, where different, smarter, and less radicalised minds prevail, maybe something revolutionarily wonderful can happen, who knows.

OPINION Chris Hughes Iran wants total Trump humiliation and strangle-hold on west

The Mirror's Chris Hughes breaks down Russia's 'glacial' advance in Ukraine

‌



View 8 Images Trump takes aim at Tehran regime (Image: China News Service via Getty Images)

"We will find out tonight, one of the most important moments in the long and complex history of the World. 47 years of extortion, corruption, and death, will finally end.”

It emerged Iran’s military, although degraded, may still have half of the missiles and drones it started with and could present a huge ‘swarm attack’ threat.

‌



Tehran hit back at Trump, warning of massive revenge attacks on America and its allies. It came in the countdown to Trump’s 1.00am GMT deadline to open the Strait of Hormuz or face ‘hell’ being unleashed.

His ‘whole civilisation’ outburst led to fears of a massive onslaught on Iran not releasing its grip on the Gulf chokepoint. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned America it had shown ‘considerable restraint.’

View 8 Images Tehran is showing no sign of backing down as Trump's deadline draws near (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



A chilling IRGC statement claimed its troops had "exercised care in selecting targets for retaliation" against the US and its regional partners.

But it vowed: "From this point forward, all such considerations will be set aside.” And it said if the US military crosses its red lines the Iranian response will ‘go beyond the region" - adding that it will target the US and its partners' infrastructure and disrupt regional oil and gas supplies for years.

US officials confirmed US forces targeted military targets on Iran's Kharg Island, which was previously targeted in March. After those strikes Trump claimed military targets had been "obliterated."

‌



Kharg Island is home to a major oil terminal, Tehran’s economic lifeline and lies about 17 miles off Iran. Trump has hinted he may send troops to seize control of the island and thousands of US assault troops are in the Gulf.

View 8 Images War-battered downtown Tehran after strike (Image: Getty Images)

Trump, asked if he is worried about committing war crimes in Iran, after threatening to attack civilian infrastructure said: “not at all.” He added: “I’m not worried about it. You know the war crime? The war crime is allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

‌



Critics have already pointed to the fact that Trump claimed his forces had totally destroyed Iran’s nuclear ambitions with an Israeli-US bombing campaign last June.

nd he Trump even said that if it were down to him, he would act like a 21st century energy pirate chief and seize Iran’s oil, but that “unfortunately, the American people would like to see us come home.

View 8 Images F-15E Strike Eagle US warplane at RAF Lakenheath, UK (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“I’d keep the oil, and I would make plenty of money,” he said. Iranian authorities have asked children to form human chains around vital infrastructure in a sick, law-defying bid to fend off looming strikes.

Officials asked "all young people, athletes, artists, students and university students and their professors" to form human chains around power plants ahead of strikes which the US president has promised.

Alireza Rahimi, identified by Iranian state television as the secretary of the Supreme Council of Youth and Adolescents, called on young Iranians to gather at the "national assets and capital".

‌



He said: "Power plants that are our national assets and capital, regardless of any taste or political viewpoint, belong to the future of Iran and to the Iranian youth." Iran has previously formed human chains around its nuclear sites.

View 8 Images Under pressure: US President Donald Trump (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

But the edict breaches the Geneva Conventions, which prohibit the coercion or direction of people to form human shields. Those same laws mean that human shields cannot further defensive aims, as infrastructure considered lawful military targets can still be targeted if civilians are present. UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned the US that attacks on civilian infrastructure are banned under international law.

‌



More than 1,900 people have died in Iran since the war began and an additional 1,400 have been killed in Lebanon. Iran has a history of using children to meet its military aims, with young Iranian boys having been pictured wearing IRGHC army fatigues.

Photographers have pictured them on camera on pro-government rallies this month as the war raged, and officials have called for children as young as 12 to join up the elite fighters.

View 8 Images Tehran under attack by the US and Israel (Image: Getty Images)

‌



On March 26 Rahim Nadali, a deputy of the IRGC Mohammad Rasoul Allah Corps of Greater Tehran, said the regime would launch a campaign called the "Homeland-Defending Combatants for Iran."

He said the programme was "open to volunteers" aged 12 and over, and encouraged them to sign up at Basij bases in mosques across Tehran.

Signing up would have seen them join "combatants defending the homeland". Some of those soldiers, Amnesty International reports, were seen at IRGC checkpoints and patrols armed with assault rifles.

Article continues below

Erika Guevara-Rosas, Senior Director for Research, Advocacy, Policy and Campaigns, said authorities are "shamelessly" encouraging children to join military service, placing them "in grave danger."

View 8 Images F-15E Strike Eagle US warplane at RAF Lakenheath (Image: Getty Images)

She said: "The Iranian authorities are shamelessly encouraging children as young as 12 to join an IRGC run military campaign, putting them in grave danger and violating international law, which prohibits the recruitment and use of children in the military. Recruiting children under 15 into the armed forces constitutes a war crime."

News.title: Hearts and Celtic given potential final-day title decider

The remaining fixtures will be staged over the weekends of 2 and 3 May, 9 and 10 May, the midweek of 12 and 13 May, with the top six finishing on 16 May and the bottom half the following day.

Amazon and the U.S. Postal Service have reportedly come to a tentative agreement regarding package handling, backing away from a potential standoff that could have seen the online retailer cut its shipping volumes by two-thirds.

The new arrangement involves a more gradual 20 percent reduction in volume, sources familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal.

This deal follows a period of friction between the two entities, during which Amazon had weighed a significant scale-back of its partnership with the national mail carrier.

The agreement is currently pending review and approval by the Postal Regulatory Commission, the federal agency that oversees USPS operations. Even with the planned reduction, the Postal Service is still on track to deliver more than 1 billion packages for Amazon each year.

The financial stakes are high for the USPS, which has come to rely on the consistent revenue provided by Amazon’s massive shipping scale. As the agency’s biggest customer, Amazon was responsible for nearly 15 percent of all USPS deliveries last year, representing approximately $6 billion in revenue for the service.

open image in gallery The new agreement arrives as the USPS continues to face significant fiscal pressure, having reported a net loss of $9 billion for the 2025 fiscal year amid two decades of ongoing deficits ( AFP/Getty )

“We’re pleased to have reached a new agreement with USPS that furthers our longstanding partnership and will let us continue supporting our customers and communities together,” an Amazon spokesperson told the outlet.

The USPS has not yet commented on the matter.

The agreement addresses potential logistical challenges for both parties. While a 66 percent cut would have been a major financial blow to the USPS, it would have also left Amazon in a difficult position.

The retailer remains heavily dependent on the Postal Service for last-mile deliveries, particularly in rural areas. Even as Amazon has been growing its own delivery network in these regions, the WSJ reported that the company would have struggled to find enough alternative capacity on such short notice.

open image in gallery Amazon would have struggled to create its own delivery network in remote regions at such short notice, the Wall Street Journal reports ( Getty )

The change in direction follows a new bidding process launched last December by Postmaster General David Steiner, aimed at establishing the true market value of the agency’s last-mile services. It was during this period that Amazon suggested the steeper 66 percent cut and began exploring options with smaller, independent carriers.

However, sources said the Postal Service decided to re-engage directly with Amazon after the projected revenue and volume from other bidders didn’t meet the agency's needs.

The USPS has faced persistent financial struggles for the better part of two decades, reporting a net loss of $9 billion for the 2025 fiscal year.

Amazon’s approach to shipping has shifted as it builds out its own logistics infrastructure. While the company once relied almost entirely on partners like FedEx and UPS, it has increasingly become a competitor to them.

Although FedEx resumed some large-scale deliveries for Amazon last year, many private carriers are still wary of becoming too dependent on a company that is both their largest customer and a primary rival.

Britain’s services sector experienced a significant slowdown in March, with a key survey indicating that geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and accelerating cost inflation are heightening the risk of “stagflation”.

The closely watched S&P Global UK services PMI survey registered a reading of 50.5 in March, a notable dip from February’s 53.9.

While this marks the lowest score recorded in 11 months, the figure remains just above the 50.0 threshold, which indicates ongoing growth within the sector.

Businesses attributed the deceleration to concerns surrounding the US-Israel conflict with Iran, which they said is stifling both business and consumer spending.

The prevailing uncertain conditions are also eroding public confidence and prompting delays in investment decisions, according to the survey findings.

Furthermore, export sales suffered a blow in March, with new international work declining at its fastest pace since April 2025, adding to the challenging economic backdrop.

The UK’s services sector had a big slowdown in March ( Getty Images )

Meanwhile, the conflict has been having a direct impact on some businesses’ cost bases due to disruption to energy infrastructure and shipping routes in the Middle East, therefore pushing up fuel costs in the UK.

This has made transportation more costly and also pushed up prices for raw materials, according to the firms surveyed.

Tim Moore, economics director for S&P Global Market Intelligence, said that the services industry experienced a “marked slowdown in output growth in March as the war in the Middle East encouraged greater risk aversion among clients and postponed investment decisions”.

He said that “stagflation risks appear to have increased”, referring to rising inflation at the same time as slower economic growth.

“Overall input cost inflation has accelerated sharply since February and was the strongest for 11 months, which was overwhelmingly linked to rising fuel and transportation bills,” Mr Moore said.

“Many firms also noted that suppliers had sought to pass on higher prices paid for energy, raw materials and shipping.”

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “The inevitable conclusion from this morning’s final PMI numbers for March is that the UK is in for another bout of stagflation, even if the conflict ends soon.

“If it drags on longer, a recession looks likely.

“We now expect the economy to stagnate for the rest of this year as higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions cause disposable income to shrink.

“Admittedly, the household saving rate is high entering the crisis, which would allow households to cushion the blow to disposable incomes by saving less, and government support may also reduce the impact on GDP (gross domestic product).”

HMS Dragon, which has been despatched to protect Britain’s air bases in Cyprus amid the Iran war, has docked in the Mediterranean after suffering technical issues.

The Royal Navy type-45 destroyer will still be able to sail at short notice “if required”, the Ministry of Defence said.

“HMS Dragon is undertaking a routine logistics stop and a short maintenance period in the eastern Mediterranean, allowing the ship to take onboard provisions, optimise systems and conduct maintenance,” an MoJ spokesperson said.

“HMS Dragon will remain at a very high level of readiness during this period, able to sail at short notice if required.

“The UK continues to maintain a robust and layered defensive presence in the eastern Mediterranean, working in coordination with allies.

“This includes Typhoon and F-35 jets, Wildcat and Merlin helicopters, and advanced counter-drone and air defence systems.”

On Tuesday, the UK urged Donald Trump to step back from his threat to wipe out “a whole civilisation” as his deadline for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz drew closer.

The US president has given Tehran until 1am on Wednesday UK time to end its blockade of the strait or face obliteration.

Downing Street again said the UK’s focus was on “de-escalation” and a “negotiated settlement” for the region, but Mr Trump ratcheted up his rhetoric and the US-Israeli bombing campaign continued.

Writing on his Truth Social platform he said: “A whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again.

“I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will.”

open image in gallery Donald Trump has threatened to bomb Iran ‘back to the Stone Ages’ if it does not reopen the Strait of Hormuz ( AP )

But Mr Trump, who has previously extended his deadline for action, said the “complete and total regime change” in Iran had resulted in a situation where “different, smarter, and less radicalised minds prevail”.

He said: “Maybe something revolutionarily wonderful can happen, WHO KNOWS? We will find out tonight, one of the most important moments in the long and complex history of the World.”

Mr Trump has said the US will destroy Iran’s bridges and power stations, saying he was “not at all” concerned that attacks on civilian infrastructure could constitute a war crime.

Asked whether the UK believed such attacks would breach international law, the prime minister’s official spokesperson said: “I’m not going to comment on [giving] a running commentary on our allies’ operations.”

The UK has granted permission for the US to use British military bases to carry out limited defensive operations, only targeting Iran’s missile sites and facilities being used to target shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital oil and gas route.

Asked whether RAF bases could be used by the US to target Iran’s civilian infrastructure, the spokesman said: “Our position has not changed.”

The spokesperson said Sir Keir Starmer had been clear “this isn’t our war” and “our position is very much focused on de-escalation”.

British director Emerald Fennell has denied that she is in negotiations to helm Amazon’s planned reboot of the 1992 erotic thriller Basic Instinct.

In a new interview with The Guardian, Joe Eszterhas — who wrote the screenplay for the original cult classic directed by Paul Verhoeven, starring Sharon Stone as a crime novelist suspected of murdering a rock star — claimed that Fennell was “in negotiations” to direct his nearly completed screenplay for the remake.

“The producers are negotiating with a really interesting director — a Brit, Emerald Fennell — who did Promising Young Woman and Wuthering Heights,” the 81-year-old writer said. “Her sensibility is exactly right. She’s someone who is not afraid of controversy and sexuality. So I’m thrilled by that. I hope it works out.”

However, Fennell’s representative quickly told Variety that “there is no truth” to Eszterhas’s claims, and that “she is not involved in any way.”

A representative for Amazon MGM Studios also shut down the claims, calling them “categorically false,” the outlet reported.

open image in gallery Sharon Stone led the 1992 cult classic ‘Basic Instinct’ ( Studio Canal )

The Independent has contacted Amazon and Fennell’s representative for further comment.

Eszterhas was reportedly paid $2 million for the new screenplay and will make another $2 million should it be made, though he remains confident that it will happen, insisting that “there’s a great demand for it. It’s trending all the time.”

Teasing the storyline for his new project, the writer said it would focus on copycat serial killers with supernatural elements.

Initially, Eszterhas wanted Stone to return for the revival, but the actor spurned the idea. “There’s not going to be a Basic Instinct reboot,” she said on the Today show last August. “I hate to break it to you, but Joe Eszterhas couldn’t write himself out of a Walgreens drug store.”

Should Fennell have directed the remake, it would have marked the Oscar-winner’s first major project since the release of her Wuthering Heights adaptation in February.

open image in gallery 'Promising Young Woman' director Emerald Fennell is ‘not involved’ in the reboot of the erotic thriller ( Getty )

Led by Margot Robbie opposite Jacob Elordi as 18th-century star-crossed lovers Catherine and Heathcliff, the film divided critics and viewers, with some finding it “emotionally hollow” and others lauding it as “oozy and wild.”

As a director, Fennell has repeatedly faced criticism for her work, with some arguing that films like Promising Young Woman and Saltburn lean on shock value and aesthetic excess.

“Promising Young Woman, her 2020 debut, in which Carey Mulligan donned a rainbow wig to kidnap and sternly tell off rapists and scumbags, was either an urgent, angry post-#MeToo battle cry, or too coy and gutless to be the revenge epic it wanted to be,” Adam White summated for The Independent earlier this year.

“Saltburn, her 2023 follow-up, was a Talented Mr Ripley riff either embraced for its shock and nudity and bodily fluids, or decried for being a toothless eat-the-rich trainwreck by Britain’s poshest writer/director. Maybe it was a bit of both.”

“Neither sparked quite as much outrage, though, as her ‘Wuthering Heights’, which seemed to generate worry and backlash from its initial announcement, straight through to its release. Now in cinemas, the film ultimately guts the messy complexity of Emily Brontë’s source material, makes the probably-not-white Heathcliff very, very white, and transforms his and Cathy Linton’s brutish dynamic of lust and loathing into basic, Fifty Shades kink.”

A record number of British children are reporting being blackmailed over sexual images of themselves, known as sextortion, with young boys accounting for almost all reports in 2025.

The Report Remove helpline, which allows children to self-report nude or sexual imagery of themselves that is circulating on the internet, received 394 reports of sextortion last year, an increase of 23 per cent from the year before.

A staggering 98 per cent of reports involving sexually coerced extortion were made by young boys, primarily aged between 14 and 17.

Hannah Swirsky, the head of policy at Internet Watch Foundation (IWF), said: “Victims and survivors of technology-facilitated child sexual abuse have talked about the stigma and the shame that can live with them for a really long time.

“Survivors have spoken about the fear they have that this imagery will continue to circulate, and the lack of control they have once that imagery is out there.”

open image in gallery The Report Remove service received 1,894 reports from children and young people last year ( PA Wire )

Ms Swirsky said that the majority of child sexual abuse material that IWF finds is of girls, which is a stark contrast to sextortion reports, which are almost entirely made by boys.

She added it was difficult to say exactly why males were making up the majority of sextortion cases, but believes the data reveals a need for more support and education aimed at helping young boys facing this abuse.

“We're calling on the government to take more steps, such as with on-device nudity detection and blocking. There are tools which can stop children from sending those images in the first place, if they've been groomed or coerced,” she said.

The Report Remove helpline was launched in 2021 and is run by the IWF in collaboration with Childline.

In 2025, the service had 1,894 instances of children and young people reporting nude or sexual imagery of themselves. The charity confirmed the presence of child sexual abuse imagery in 1,175 of these reports, an 83 per cent rise compared to 2024.

More than a third of the reports made involved sextortion, which can often include financial sexual extortion, where a criminal threatens to share sexual imagery online if the victim does not pay them money. It also includes victims being coerced into sending more images of themselves to prevent the criminal from sharing the original content.

The IWF identified 2,963 child sexual abuse images and 509 videos last year.

open image in gallery Safeguarding minister Jess Phillips said growing numbers of children were being harmed by sextortion ( PA Wire )

Childline director Shaun Friel said: “Our counsellors hear from young people who are being blackmailed into sharing videos of themselves, as well as being threatened that their intimate images might be shared with friends, family or their school unless they pay money or send more content. For many, the fear and isolation can feel overwhelming, and they often struggle to tell a trusted adult about what’s happening.

“The rise is contacts to Report Remove about sextortion leaves us with mixed feelings. Obviously, it is worrying to see further evidence of how serious a problem this now is, but at the same time it is positive that there is greater awareness about the service and children are more willing to get in touch and seek help.”

Jess Phillips, the minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, said: “Child sexual abuse and sextortion are devastating crimes, harming growing numbers of children across the world, and leaving scars that can last a lifetime.

“Too often, fear, embarrassment and shame have tragically driven children to suicide. That reality weighs heavily on me every single day and I will do everything I can to make the online world safer for our children.”
